馬特諾電子波琴屬電鳴樂器，發聲不靠本體共振，而以電流產生頻率，經放大與揚聲器轉成: The ondes Martenot is an electrophone: it does not sound through the resonance of a body, but generates a frequency electrically and turns it into a sound wave through amplification and a loudspeaker. Early models used a ring slid along a wire, and the timbre was close to the theremin's; a keyboard was added later, and its keys move from side to side to make a vibrato, which keeps the pitch steadier. Later instruments can produce sine, triangle, square and pulse waves, a full-wave rectified sine and pink noise at once, and the volume is controlled by the touch-sensitive glass strip in the left-hand drawer and by the master volume knob. The keyboard range is about C1 to C8.
馬特諾電子波琴為電鳴樂器，由法國人莫里斯·馬特諾於1928年發明並申請專利。早期: The ondes Martenot is an electrophone, invented and patented by the Frenchman Maurice Martenot in 1928. Early models sounded by sliding a ring along a wire; in 1929 the third model added a non-functional keyboard as an indication, in the 1930s the fourth model introduced a keyboard that moved sideways to produce a vibrato, and later models settled at 72 keys. After the premiere at the Paris Opera in 1928, Martenot toured Europe and New York, and at the 1937 Paris World's Fair as many as twelve players demonstrated the instrument; from 1947 it was taught at the Paris Conservatoire. It declined because it was never mass-produced; in the 1970s the seventh model replaced the vacuum tubes with integrated circuit boards, production stopped in 1988, and an improved version of 1998 is called the Ondéa.
馬特諾電子波琴用於逾百首管弦樂作品，也出現在電影、電視配樂，尤其科幻與恐怖類型。: The ondes Martenot has been used in more than a hundred orchestral works, and also in film and television scores, especially of science fiction and horror. Messiaen sets it beside the piano and a large orchestra in the Turangalîla Symphony, and also uses it in La fête des belles eaux, the Trois petites liturgies de la présence divine and Saint François d'Assise. Honegger's Jeanne d'Arc au bûcher uses it to strengthen the string section, and Varèse replaced the theremin part with it in the premiere of Amériques and in Ecuatorial. Today it appears in the work of Daft Punk, Damon Albarn and Radiohead's Jonny Greenwood.
馬特諾電子波琴的演奏以右手為主：早期可站立拉動連接木盒的金屬線，後期則戴金屬環沿: Playing the ondes Martenot is mainly done with the right hand: in the early period the player stood and pulled a metal wire attached to a wooden box, while later players wear a metal ring and slide it along the wire, or play on the keyboard, whose sideways movement produces a vibrato. The left hand works the drawer on the left of the instrument to set volume and timbre; the volume can be controlled by the touch-sensitive glass strip. Martenot's teaching manual of 1931 already covers both the ring and the keyboard methods, and a beginner should first master the glissando, a steady pitch and the control of the drawer.
馬特諾電子波琴的結構由木製外殼組成，通常採用高級木材製作，內部安裝電子振盪器與放: The ondes Martenot has a wooden case, usually of a fine wood, with the oscillator and amplifier electronics inside. The keyboard is ivory or plastic, and the control ring is metal. Inside the instrument are vacuum-tube circuits, transformers and other electronic components, and the controls in the outer drawer are metal mechanical parts. The loudspeaker units use a metal frame and a paper cone, so that the whole instrument joins woodwork to precision electronics.

The ondes Martenot is an early electronic instrument, invented in 1928 by the Frenchman Maurice Martenot and classified as an electrophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 531.1. The player can wear a metal ring and slide it along the wire to make a glissando, or play the sideways-moving keyboard and produce a vibrato; the drawer on the left controls volume and timbre. The sound is generated by an oscillating circuit and comes out through a loudspeaker. It is much used in orchestral music, opera, and film and television scores, and it also appears in contemporary pop and rock; Messiaen, Jeanne Loriod and Jonny Greenwood are all associated with the instrument.
